title: Is it OK to bring iced coffee to a job interview?
description:
Would you bring an iced coffee to a job interview? A viral TikTok from Caitlin Wehniainen - a recruiter in Florida - has stirred up a huge debate. It’s after she said that Gen Z candidates turning up to job interviews with an iced coffee can look too casual and unprofessional.

But seriously…can an iced latte actually hurt your chances of getting a job? And what does your coffee order have to do with whether you’d be good at it? Grab your drink of choice because we’re getting into it with BBC reporters Baldeep Chahal, Leona Gasper and Stefania Okereke from the What in the World team. BBC journalist Sanjana Idnani tells us about the difficult job market recent graduates are having to contend with. And BBC reporter Basma El Atti shares her thoughts from Nairobi.

Plus: We get hot takes from content creators Alexis Wilson (@sucseed_academics), Olivia Monday (@oliviamonday_) and Piper Phillips (@piperphillips) from Instagram, and Coka (@cokafree), Anne-Tso @theportfoliocareercoach, Evan (@thisamericanmess) from TikTok.

Instagram: @bbcwhatintheworld Email: whatintheworld@bbc.co.uk WhatsApp: +44 330 12 33 22 6 Presenter: William Lee Adams Producer: Baldeep Chahal Editor: Verity Wilde
summaryZh: 本集 BBC 節目《What in the World》探討求職者是否可以攜帶冰咖啡參加工作面試的爭議。這場討論源於美國佛羅里達州招募人員在 TikTok 影片中的觀點，她認為 Z 世代求職者手拿冰拿鐵面試顯得過於隨意且不專業。節目邀請 BBC 記者與多位創作者分享不同觀點：反對者指出帶飲料面試違反職場禮儀、容易造成桌面水痕與噪音，甚至被視為挑戰權威；支持者則認為喝咖啡有助於舒緩緊張，不應被過度解讀。節目進一步探討了在高青年失業率背景下，不同世代對職場「專業」定義的歧異。
summaryEn: This episode examines the online debate over whether bringing an iced coffee to a job interview is acceptable or unprofessional. Sparked by a viral TikTok video from a Florida recruiter who argued that holding an iced drink looks too casual and signals disrespect for authority, the episode features discussions among BBC reporters and social media creators. Opponents argue that bringing a beverage breaches corporate etiquette, creates mess and distraction, and risks giving a negative first impression in a competitive job market. Conversely, supporters—particularly among Gen Z—view it as a harmless comfort measure and challenge overly rigid workplace norms. The episode also contextualizes the debate within high youth unemployment rates and shifting generational expectations around professionalism.
